claim: Plasma TMA levels are significantly elevated in moderate and severe AH patients compared to healthy controls.
source: Plasma TMA (A) and trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) (B) levels in patients considered healthy (n = 13 for TMA and 20 for TMAO), or who have moderate (MELD < 20) (n = 52 for TMA and 111 for TMAO) or severe (MELD > 20) (n = 83 for TMA and 152 for TMAO) AH.
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1A demonstrate elevated TMA levels in AH patients measured by LC-MS/MS.

claim: TMAO levels are reciprocally decreased in AH patients compared to healthy controls.
source: However, the CVD-related co-metabolite TMAO was reciprocally decreased in AH patients (Figure 1B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows decreased TMAO levels in AH patients measured by mass spectrometry.

claim: FMO3 mRNA levels are uniquely repressed in patients with more severe AH but not in other liver disease etiologies such as NAFLD or viral hepatitis.
source: Interestingly, mRNA levels for FMO3 are uniquely repressed in patients with more severe AH (AH with liver failure [MELD 22–28] and AH with emergency liver transplant [MELD 18–21]), but not in other liver disease etiologies such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) or viral hepatitis (Figure 1C).
evidence: RNA sequencing data from liver tissues of patients with different pathologies shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Patients with severe AH undergoing emergency liver transplant have marked reduction in FMO3 protein.
source: In agreement with reduced mRNA levels (Figure 1C), patients with severe AH undergoing emergency liver transplant have marked reduction in FMO3 protein (Figure 1D), which likely contributes to elevations in plasma TMA (Figure 1A).
evidence: Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1D demonstrates reduced FMO3 protein in severe AH patients.

claim: A single injection of LPS to induce acute hepatic inflammation is associated with both a reduction in the expression of Fmo3 and a significant increase in the TMA receptor Taar5.
source: Although ethanol feeding in mice does not consistently result in reduced hepatic Fmo3 expression (data not shown), a single injection of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to induce acute hepatic inflammation is associated with both a reduction in the expression of Fmo3 and a significant increase in the TMA receptor trace amine-associated receptor 5 (Taar5) (Figure 1E).
evidence: qPCR data from LPS-injected mice shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Circulating choline levels were not significantly altered in patients with AH compared to healthy controls.
source: It is important to note that circulating choline levels was not significantly altered in patients with AH compared to healthy controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plasma levels of carnitine, betaine, and γ-butyrobetaine were elevated in patients with AH compared to healthy controls.
source: However, plasma levels of one of the gut microbial substrates for TMA production (carnitine) and other TMA pathway co-metabolites (e.g. betaine and γ-butyrobetaine) were elevated in patients with AH compared to healthy controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: IMC treatment effectively blunted ethanol-induced increases in plasma TMA and TMAO.
source: IMC treatment effectively blunted ethanol-induced increases in plasma TMA and TMAO (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data from IMC-treated mice shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: IMC prevented ethanol-induced increases in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and hepatic steatosis.
source: IMC also prevented ethanol-induced increases in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and hepatic steatosis (Figure 2F, G, and K).
evidence: Enzymatic assays and histological analysis shown in Figure 2F, G, and K.

claim: IMC treatment prevented ethanol-induced increases in hepatic triglycerides.
source: Interestingly, IMC treatment prevented ethanol-induced increases in hepatic triglycerides (Figure 2G), and reduced hepatic total and cholesterol esters, but not free cholesterol, in both pair- and ethanol-fed conditions (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: Enzymatic measurements of liver lipids shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: IMC treatment reduced the expression levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor α (Tnfα).
source: IMC treatment also reduced the expression levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor α (Tnfα) (Figure 2L).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: IMC treatment resulted in an unexpected reduction in food intake and body weights in mice receiving both IMC and ethanol.
source: Although IMC was well tolerated in several previous mouse studies in the setting of standard rodent chow-feeding (Roberts et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2020; Organ et al., 2020), here we found an unexpected reduction in food intake and body weights in mice receiving both IMC and ethanol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Body weight and food intake measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: FMC treatment was well tolerated and did not significantly alter liquid diet intake or body weights throughout the 25-day chronic ethanol feeding study.
source: Importantly, FMC was well tolerated and did not significantly alter liquid diet intake or body weights throughout the 25-day chronic ethanol feeding study (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Body weight and diet intake measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: FMC treatment trended toward reducing plasma TMA and more dramatically suppressed plasma TMAO levels.
source: FMC treatment trended toward reducing plasma TMA (Figure 3A), and more dramatically suppressed plasma TMAO levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data from FMC-treated mice shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: FMC treatment significantly protected against ethanol-induced ALT elevations and hepatic steatosis.
source: More importantly, as with IMC (Figure 2F–K), FMC treatment significantly protected against ethanol-induced ALT elevations (Figure 3F), hepatic steatosis (Figure 3G and K), and reduced total and esterified cholesterol levels without altering free cholesterol (Figure 3H–J).
evidence: Enzymatic assays and histological analysis shown in Figure 3F-K.

claim: Both IMC and FMC promoted clear restructuring of the cecal microbiome in an ethanol-dependent manner.
source: Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) of microbial taxa revealed distinct clusters, indicating that both IMC and FMC promoted clear restructuring of the cecal microbiome in an ethanol-dependent manner (Figure 4A and F).
evidence: 16S rRNA sequencing data and NMDS analysis shown in Figure 4A and F.

claim: Under pair-feeding conditions, both IMC and FMC caused a reciprocal decrease in the relative abundance of Bacteroidetes and increase in Firmicutes.
source: Under pair-feeding conditions, both IMC and FMC caused a reciprocal decrease in the relative abundance of Bacteroidetes and increase in Firmicutes (Figure 4B and G).
evidence: 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B and G.

claim: Under ethanol-fed conditions IMC resulted in increased Bacteroidetes and reduced Firmicutes.
source: However, under ethanol-fed conditions IMC resulted in increased Bacteroidetes and reduced Firmicutes, and FMC treatment resulted in more modest reductions in Bacteroidetes and increased Firmicutes (Figure 4B and G).
evidence: 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B and G.

claim: Under both pair- and ethanol-fed conditions, IMC treatment promoted significant increases in Faecalibaculum and Escherichica/Shigella, and reductions in Bacteroidales_S24-7.
source: When examining drug-specific alterations at the genus level, we found that under both pair- and ethanol-fed conditions, IMC treatment promoted significant increases in Faecalibaculum and Escherichica/Shigella, and reductions in Bacteroidales_S24-7 (Figure 4C–E , and H–I).
evidence: 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4C-E and H-I.

claim: FMC most significantly altered Turicibacter, Oscillibacter, and Lachnospiraceae, and these FMC-induced alterations were different between pair- and ethanol-fed groups.
source: FMC, however, most significantly altered Turicibacter, Oscillibacter, and Lachnospiraceae, and it is important to note that these FMC-induced alterations were different between pair- and ethanol-fed groups (Figure 4C–E , and H–I).
evidence: 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4C-E and H-I.

claim: NMDS and hierarchical clustering analysis of liver RNA sequencing showed clear separation between all four groups (pair, ethanol, pair+IMC, ethanol+IMC).
source: NMDS and hierarchical clustering analysis showed clear separation between all four groups (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: RNA sequencing data and NMDS analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In pair-fed mice, IMC treatment caused significant decreases in several genes encoding major urinary proteins and cytochrome p450 enzymes, while increasing other genes involved in xenobiotic metabolism and hormone/cytokine signaling.
source: In pair-fed mice, IMC treatment caused significant decreases in several genes encoding major urinary proteins (Mup2, Mup10, Mup11, and Mup18) and cytochrome p450 enzymes (Cyp3a16, Cyp3a44), while increasing other genes involved in xenobiotic metabolism (Ephx1, Cyp4a31) and hormone/cytokine signaling (Lepr, Fgf21, Il22ra1) (Figure 5C).
evidence: RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Under ethanol-feeding conditions, IMC treatment most significantly altered genes involved in hepatocyte metabolism, RNA processing, and major urinary proteins.
source: Under ethanol-feeding conditions, IMC treatment most significantly altered genes involved in hepatocyte metabolism (Cyp8b1, Ugt1a5, Pnpla5, Sult2a8, Ces3a, and Cmah), RNA processing (Ddx21, Ftsj3, Dus1l, and Cmah), and again major urinary proteins (Mup2, Mup10, Mup11, and Mup20) (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: A total of 36 liver proteins exhibited site-specific hypo- or hyper-phosphorylation 10 min after administration of TMA relative to vehicle-injected mice.
source: A total of 36 liver proteins exhibited site-specific hypo- or hyper-phosphorylation 10 min after administration of TMA relative to vehicle-injected mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: Phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Portal vein infusion of TMA resulted in altered phosphorylation of proteins implicated in protein kinase A (PKA) signaling, including AKAP1 and FKBP15.
source: For example, portal vein infusion of TMA resulted in altered phosphorylation of proteins implicated in protein kinase A (PKA) signaling, including A kinase anchor protein 1 (AKAP1) (Huang et al., 1999) and FK506-binding protein 15 (FKBP15) (Nooh and Bahouth, 2017), and insulin signaling including insulin receptor substrate 2 (IRS2) (Araki et al., 1994; Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 6B-D with supporting citations.

claim: TMA infusion was associated with altering the phosphorylation of several guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEF), including Arhgef6 and ARHGAP17.
source: TMA infusion was also associated with altering the phosphorylation of several guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEF), including Rac/Cdc42 guanine nucleotide exchange factor 6 (Arhgef6) and Rho GTPase activating protein 17 (ARHGAP17) (Zhou et al., 2016; Aslan, 2019), and proteins involved in RNA processing/splicing including signal recognition particle 14 (SRP14) (Strub and Walter, 1990) and serine- and arginine-rich splicing factor 1 (SRSF1) (Cho et al., 2011; Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 6B and C with supporting citations.

claim: Shortly after diagnosis AH patients die at a staggering rate of 40–50%.
source: Shortly after diagnosis AH patients die at a staggering rate of 40–50% (Masarone et al., 2016; Kochanek et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Masarone et al., 2016; Kochanek et al., 2017).

claim: AH has consistently been linked to reorganization of the gut microbiome and dysregulation of microbe-host interactions.
source: Similar to other components of the spectrum of ALD, AH has consistently been linked to reorganization of the gut microbiome and dysregulation of microbe-host interactions (Chen et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2011; Mutlu et al., 2009; Mutlu et al., 2012; Tripathi et al., 2018; Ciocan et al., 2018; Llopis et al., 2016; Duan et al., 2019; Smirnova et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2019; Puri et al., 2018; Lang and Schnabl, 2020).
evidence: Cited from multiple published studies.

claim: Chronic alcohol use can elicit structural alterations in the gut barrier, allowing either live bacteria themselves or microbe-associated molecule patterns (MAMPs) to enter the portal circulation.
source: It is well appreciated that chronic alcohol use can elicit structural alterations in the gut barrier, allowing either live bacteria themselves or microbe-associated molecule patterns (MAMPs), such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS), to enter the portal circulation where they can directly engage pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs) or NOD-like receptors (NLRP3, NLRP6, etc.) to promote hepatic inflammation and tissue injury (Wilkinson et al., 1974; Tarao et al., 1979; Uesugi et al., 2001; Paik et al., 2003; DeSantis et al., 2013; Knorr et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from multiple published studies.

claim: Gut microbes can act as a collective endocrine organ, producing a vast array of small molecules, proteins, and lipid metabolites that can engage dedicated host receptor systems to impact liver disease progression.
source: In addition to MAMP-PRR interactions, gut microbes can act as a collective endocrine organ, producing a vast array of small molecules, proteins, and lipid metabolites that can engage dedicated host receptor systems to also impact liver disease progression (Brown and Hazen, 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Brown and Hazen, 2015).

claim: Breath levels of TMA and other related co-metabolites are elevated in patients with ALD.
source: Although the gut microbial TMAO pathway has been studied mostly in the context of CVD (Wang et al., 2011; Koeth et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014b; Trøseid et al., 2015; Tang and Hazen, 2014), recent studies found that breath levels of the primary metabolite TMA and other related co-metabolites are elevated in patients with ALD (Hanouneh et al., 2014; Ascha et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published studies (Hanouneh et al., 2014; Ascha et al., 2016).

claim: FMO3 is the predominant TMA to TMAO converting enzyme in the adult liver.
source: Given the reciprocal alterations in plasma TMA and TMAO levels, we next examined the expression of the host liver enzyme flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 (FMO3) which is the predominant TMA to TMAO converting enzyme in the adult liver (Cashman, 2002).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Cashman, 2002).

claim: IMC and FMC are designed as suicide substrate mechanism-based inhibitors.
source: Designed as suicide substrate mechanism-based inhibitors, past studies reveal that the vast majority of IMC and FMC is retained in the gut within luminal bacteria and excreted in the feces with limited systemic exposure of the polar drug in the host (Roberts et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2020; Organ et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from previous published studies (Roberts et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2020; Organ et al., 2020).

claim: The vast majority of IMC and FMC is retained in the gut within luminal bacteria and excreted in the feces with limited systemic exposure of the polar drug in the host.
source: Designed as suicide substrate mechanism-based inhibitors, past studies reveal that the vast majority of IMC and FMC is retained in the gut within luminal bacteria and excreted in the feces with limited systemic exposure of the polar drug in the host (Roberts et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2020; Organ et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from previous published studies (Roberts et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2020; Organ et al., 2020).

claim: Small molecule inhibition of the gut microbial transformation of choline into TMA can significantly reduce disease burden in animal models of atherosclerosis, thrombosis, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease.
source: In fact, we have recently shown that small molecule inhibition of the gut microbial transformation of choline into trimethylamine (TMA), the initial and rate-limiting step in the generation of the cardiovascular disease (CVD)-associated metabolite trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), can significantly reduce disease burden in animal models of atherosclerosis, thrombosis, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease (Roberts et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2020; Organ et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from previous published studies (Roberts et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2020; Organ et al., 2020).

claim: MELD score, Maddrey's discriminant function score, Child-Pugh score, AST, total bilirubin, creatinine, and international normalized ratio were higher in patients with severe AH compared to moderate AH patients.
source: Importantly, MELD score, Maddrey's discriminant function score, Child-Pugh score, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), total bilirubin, creatinine, and international normalized ratio were higher in patients with severe AH compared to moderate AH patients, while serum albumin was lower in severe AH compared to moderate AH patients.
evidence: Clinical characteristics summarized from patient cohort data in Figure 1—source data 1 and 2.

claim: Serum albumin was lower in severe AH compared to moderate AH patients.
source: Importantly, MELD score, Maddrey's discriminant function score, Child-Pugh score, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), total bilirubin, creatinine, and international normalized ratio were higher in patients with severe AH compared to moderate AH patients, while serum albumin was lower in severe AH compared to moderate AH patients.
evidence: Clinical characteristics summarized from patient cohort data in Figure 1—source data 1 and 2.

claim: Reduced hepatic FMO3 expression likely contributes to elevations in plasma TMA in severe AH patients.
source: In agreement with reduced mRNA levels (Figure 1C), patients with severe AH undergoing emergency liver transplant have marked reduction in FMO3 protein (Figure 1D), which likely contributes to elevations in plasma TMA (Figure 1A).
evidence: Inferred from the reciprocal relationship between reduced FMO3 (enzyme that converts TMA to TMAO) and elevated TMA levels.

claim: TMA and related co-metabolites may allow for discrimination of AH from other liver diseases.
source: These findings, in addition to previous breath metabolomic studies (Hanouneh et al., 2014; Ascha et al., 2016), provide evidence that TMA and related co-metabolites may allow for discrimination of AH from other liver diseases.
evidence: Based on data showing unique elevation of TMA in AH and unique suppression of FMO3 in severe AH compared to other liver diseases, combined with cited breath metabolomics studies.

claim: Gut microbe-targeted choline TMA lyase inhibition with two structurally distinct inhibitors (IMC or FMC) can generally protect mice against ethanol-induced liver injury.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that gut microbe-targeted choline TMA lyase inhibition with two structurally distinct inhibitors (IMC or FMC) can generally protect mice against ethanol-induced liver injury.
evidence: Summary statement based on data from Figures 2 and 3 showing protection with both inhibitors.

claim: Inhibition of gut microbial choline to TMA transformation with a selective non-lethal small molecule inhibitor promotes restructuring of the gut microbiome in an ethanol-dependent manner.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that inhibition of gut microbial choline to TMA transformation with a selective non-lethal small molecule inhibitor promotes restructuring of the gut microbiome in an ethanol-dependent manner.
evidence: Summary statement based on 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Gut microbe-targeted choline TMA lyase inhibitors can alter the host liver transcriptome in an ethanol feeding-dependent manner.
source: These unbiased RNASeq data demonstrate that gut microbe-targeted choline TMA lyase inhibitors can alter the host liver transcriptome in an ethanol feeding-dependent manner.
evidence: Summary statement based on RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The gut microbe-derived co-metabolites TMA and TMAO are generated postprandially in both rodents and humans after a substrate-rich meal is ingested.
source: The gut microbe-derived co-metabolites TMA and TMAO are generated postprandially in both rodents and humans after a substrate-rich meal is ingested (Schugar et al., 2018; Boutagy et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from published studies (Schugar et al., 2018; Boutagy et al., 2015).

claim: TMA may be acting as a gut microbe-derived hormone to promote liver injury.
source: Given the acute meal-related production and recent identification of candidate host receptors for TMA (Li et al., 2013; Wallrabenstein et al., 2013) and TMAO (Chen et al., 2019), we hypothesized that TMA may be acting as a gut microbe-derived hormone to promote liver injury.
evidence: Hypothesis based on postprandial production of TMA and existence of host receptors cited from literature (Li et al., 2013; Wallrabenstein et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2019).

claim: Direct administration of TMA can elicit rapid signaling effects in the liver.
source: Here, we also show for the first time that a selective non-lethal small molecule drug that reduces bacterial production of TMA can prevent ethanol-induced liver injury in mice. We also demonstrate that direct administration of TMA can elicit rapid signaling effects in the liver, supporting the notion that gut microbial metabolites produced postprandially can act in an endocrine-like manner to alter host signal transduction and associated disease pathogenesis.
evidence: Summary statement based on phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Gut microbial metabolites produced postprandially can act in an endocrine-like manner to alter host signal transduction and associated disease pathogenesis.
source: We also demonstrate that direct administration of TMA can elicit rapid signaling effects in the liver, supporting the notion that gut microbial metabolites produced postprandially can act in an endocrine-like manner to alter host signal transduction and associated disease pathogenesis.
evidence: Inference based on phosphoproteomics data showing rapid TMA-induced signaling changes in liver.

claim: Selective drugs targeting the gut microbial TMA pathway may hold promise for treating AH.
source: Collectively, these studies suggest that selective drugs targeting the gut microbial TMA pathway may hold promise for treating AH.
evidence: Conclusion based on data showing elevated TMA in AH patients and protective effects of TMA lyase inhibitors in mouse models.

claim: Both IMC and FMC similarly improved ethanol-induced liver injury despite having some consistent but many different cecal microbiome alterations.
source: In the current studies there were some consistent, but many different cecal microbiome alterations when comparing IMC and FMC (Figure 4), yet both drugs similarly improved ethanol-induced liver injury.
evidence: Comparison of microbiome data (Figure 4) and liver injury data (Figures 2 and 3) for both inhibitors.

claim: Some of the beneficial effects of bacterial enzyme inhibitors will originate from the restructuring of gut microbiome communities.
source: As small molecule bacterial enzymes inhibitors are developed, it will be extremely important to understand their effects on microbial ecology, and it is expected that some of the beneficial effects of these drugs will indeed originate from the restructuring of gut microbiome communities.
evidence: Speculation based on observed microbiome restructuring with inhibitor treatment.

claim: Nearly a quarter of commonly used host-targeted drugs have microbiome-altering properties.
source: In fact, this is not an uncommon mechanism by which host targeted drugs impact human health. A recent study showed that nearly a quarter of commonly used host-targeted drugs have microbiome-altering properties (Maier et al., 2018), and in the context of diabetes therapeutics it is important to note metformin's anti-diabetic effects are partially mediated by the drug's microbiome altering properties (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from published studies (Maier et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2017).

claim: Metformin's anti-diabetic effects are partially mediated by the drug's microbiome altering properties.
source: A recent study showed that nearly a quarter of commonly used host-targeted drugs have microbiome-altering properties (Maier et al., 2018), and in the context of diabetes therapeutics it is important to note metformin's anti-diabetic effects are partially mediated by the drug's microbiome altering properties (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from published study (Wu et al., 2017).

claim: The gut microbial TMA/TMAO pathway represents only one of many microbial metabolic circuits that have been associated with human disease.
source: The metaorganismal TMA/TMAO pathway represents only one of many microbial metabolic circuits that have been associated with human disease (Figure 7). In fact, many microbe-associated metabolites such as short chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, phenolic acids, polyamines, and others have more recently been associated with many human diseases (Brown and Hazen, 2015; Gilbert et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from published reviews (Brown and Hazen, 2015; Gilbert et al., 2018).

claim: Gut microbes produce a diverse array of metabolites that reach micromolar to millimolar concentrations in the blood in an ethanol- and meal-related manner.
source: In an ethanol- and meal-related manner, gut microbes produce a diverse array of metabolites that reach micromolar to millimolar concentrations in the blood, making the collective gut microbiome an active endocrine organ (Brown and Hazen, 2015).
evidence: Cited from published review (Brown and Hazen, 2015).

claim: Diet/ethanol-microbe-host metabolic interplay can be causally linked to ethanol-induced liver injury.
source: Small molecule metabolites are well known to be mediators of signaling interactions in the host, and this work provides evidence that diet/ethanol-microbe-host metabolic interplay can be causally linked to ethanol-induced liver injury.
evidence: Conclusion based on data showing TMA elevation in AH patients and protective effects of inhibiting TMA production in mice.

claim: There is clear evidence of bi-directional crosstalk between the gut microbial endocrine organ and host liver metabolism.
source: Our work, and that of many others, demonstrates that there is clear evidence of bi-directional crosstalk between the gut microbial endocrine organ and host liver metabolism.
evidence: Summary statement based on data from this study and cited literature.

claim: Non-lethal gut microbe-targeted enzyme inhibitors may serve as effective therapeutics in AH.
source: This work highlights that non-lethal gut microbe-targeted enzyme inhibitors may serve as effective therapeutics in AH and provides proof of concept that this may be a generalizable approach to target metaorganismal crosstalk in other disease contexts.
evidence: Conclusion based on data showing protective effects of IMC and FMC in mouse models of ethanol-induced liver injury.

claim: Selective inhibition of bacterial enzymes has the advantage over host targeting given that small molecules can be designed to avoid systemic absorption and exposure, thereby minimizing potential host off target effects.
source: In fact, selective inhibition of bacterial enzymes has the advantage over host targeting given that small molecules can be designed to avoid systemic absorption and exposure, thereby minimizing potential host off target effects.
evidence: Reasoning based on the pharmacokinetic properties of gut-restricted bacterial enzyme inhibitors.

claim: Other microbe-host interactions are mechanistically linked to host disease pathogenesis and can serve as the basis for the rational design of microbe-targeted therapeutics.
source: As shown here with the gut microbial TMA/TMAO pathway, it is easy to envision that other microbe-host interactions are mechanistically linked to host disease pathogenesis, serving as the basis for the rational design of microbe-targeted therapeutics that improve human health.
evidence: Extrapolation from the TMA/TMAO pathway findings to other potential microbe-host interactions.

claim: Intestinal microbes metabolize dietary L-carnitine, choline, or phosphatidylcholine (PC) to form TMA.
source: Relevant to this manuscript, intestinal microbes metabolize dietary L-carnitine, choline, or phosphatidylcholine (PC) to form TMA, which is a volatile compound that originates exclusively from gut bacterial metabolism and is elevated in ALD.
evidence: Established knowledge about the TMA pathway depicted in Figure 7.

claim: TMA is a volatile compound that originates exclusively from gut bacterial metabolism.
source: Relevant to this manuscript, intestinal microbes metabolize dietary L-carnitine, choline, or phosphatidylcholine (PC) to form TMA, which is a volatile compound that originates exclusively from gut bacterial metabolism and is elevated in ALD.
evidence: Established knowledge about TMA production.

claim: TMA can be converted to TMAO by hepatic FMO3.
source: Importantly, TMA can also be converted to trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) by hepatic flavin monooxygenase 3 (FMO3), and TMAO has recently been linked to cardiovascular disease (CVD) promotion in humans.
evidence: Established knowledge about the TMA to TMAO conversion pathway.

claim: TMAO has been linked to cardiovascular disease (CVD) promotion in humans.
source: Importantly, TMA can also be converted to trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) by hepatic flavin monooxygenase 3 (FMO3), and TMAO has recently been linked to cardiovascular disease (CVD) promotion in humans.
evidence: Established knowledge from previous studies on TMAO and CVD.

claim: Gut hyperpermeability (leaky gut) allows bacterial cell wall products such as LPS and peptidoglycans to enter into the blood stream and engage with host pattern recognition receptors (PRR) to promote hepatic inflammation.
source: Metabolism-independent effects are the result of gut hyperpermeability (leaky gut), allowing bacterial cell wall products such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and peptidoglycans to enter into the blood stream and engage with host pattern recognition receptors (PRR) to promote hepatic inflammation.
evidence: Established knowledge about the leaky gut mechanism in ALD depicted in Figure 7.

claim: The small molecule bacterially targeted CutC/D inhibitors IMC and FMC can effectively blunt ethanol-induced liver injury in mice.
source: The small molecule bacterially targeted CutC/D inhibitors iodomethylcholine (IMC) and fluoromethylcholine (FMC) can effectively blunt ethanol-induced liver injury in mice.
evidence: Summary statement based on data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Metabolism-dependent pathways such as TMA production as well as metabolism-independent pathways provide multiple bacterially derived 'hits' to promote ALD progression.
source: Collectively, metabolism-dependent pathways such as TMA production as well as metabolism-independent pathways provide multiple bacterially derived 'hits' to promote ALD progression.
evidence: Summary statement integrating both mechanisms depicted in Figure 7.
